 Gov. Jared Polis unveils outline for 2027-28 state budget
 By Marianne Goodland 
 Published November 2, 2026 2:56pm 
 | Updated November 2, 2026 4:17pm 
 + Add Colorado Politics on Google 
 Gov. Jared Polis, joined by his budget director, Mark Ferrandino and Lt. Gov. Dianne Primavera, presents his proposal for the 2027-28 budget. 
 Gov. Jared Polis unveiled his eighth and final proposed state budget Monday for the 2027-28 fiscal year, though the spending plan is expected to change significantly before it is finalized.
 State law requires the governor to submit a balanced budget proposal for the upcoming fiscal year by about Nov. 1. While Monday’s proposal serves as the starting point for the budget process, it is far from the finished product.

 Polis will release an updated budget proposal on Jan. 2, 2027. Final decisions, however, will fall to the legislature and the governor elected to succeed him.
 The 2027-28 budget as proposed by Polis is $51.2 billion, about $579 million more than the 2026-27 budget. General fund dollars, one of three sources of funds for the budget and the money that is the most discretionary, makes up $18.9 billion, which is $479 million more than the 2026-27 budget.
 The largest increase is for caseload, which can be for Medicaid or corrections, for example, at $580 million, with an increase of $498 million in general fund dollars.
 Medicaid
 Medicaid is the biggest budget item, administered through the Colorado Department of Health Care Policy and Financing. That department now takes 38% of the general fund budget, overtaking spending on corrections and education in recent years. 
 But Polis’ presentation to reporters Monday didn’t outline how much he proposes to spend.
 Based on current spending trends, Polis said Medicaid spending would increase by 15% in the 2027-28 budget.
 They propose capping the growth rate at 4.3%, the TABOR growth rate. That 4.3% would cost the state $820 million more in total funds and $250 million in general fund dollars. Polis told reporters they are looking for federal and other non-general fund resources.
 A budget document from the Office of State Planning and Budgeting shows HCPF’s total budget at nearly $21 billion, with Medicaid funded at about $16 billion, including $9.2 billion in federal funds.
 SNAP
 As of Oct. 1, 2027, under federal H.R. 1 legislation from 2025, Colorado and other states will be required to cover 50% of the cost of administering SNAP benefits, which are food stamps. That will require an additional $100 million to cover those costs.
 According to Polis, that money could come from another measure referred to the General Assembly: boosting the amount of money the state can keep through its Healthy School Meals for All program.
 That ballot measure, first approved by voters in 2022 , has consistently brought in more money than originally projected. Households with incomes above $300,000 annually pay for the program, with a lower limit on standard or itemized deductions.
 In 2025, voters were asked once again to increase the limit on what the state can collect and to use some of those funds for SNAP benefits. 
 The program still exceeded its statutorily created limits by $30 million in 2025-26, and Polis suggested another ballot measure to allow the state to keep that money to help pay for increased SNAP costs.
 The budget proposal did not outline how to address a looming $1.6 billion budget shortfall. Polis, however, continues to consider privatizing Pinnacol Assurance, the state’s largest workers’ compensation insurer, as a way to shore up the state’s general fund reserve.
 A description of the proposal from the Office of State Planning and Budgeting shows the state would collect $400 million if the company were allowed to privatize, with half going to shore up the general fund reserve. Another $100 million would go to the state’s childcare program.
 Colorado Concern proposed a ballot measure for 2026 but pulled it after indicating it would wait for a legislative solution. Some Joint Budget Committee members, however, have been lukewarm on the policy.
 Property taxes
 The governor’s budget also proposes eliminating the business personal property tax reimbursement for counties, which will require legislation.
 In 2017, lawmakers passed an omnibus bill known as “ sustainability of rural Colorado.” That bill included the business personal property tax reimbursement Republicans had sought for at least a decade, a tax credit that largely goes to small businesses.
 For 2026, the tax credit covers taxes imposed on the first $18,000 of the total actual value of business personal property. That’s things like machinery, equipment, furniture and most other personal property retained by the business. 
 In 2025, the state reimbursed counties and other local taxing districts nearly $19.5 million in tax credits, with $10 million coming through school districts.
 Polis said they’re eliminating the state’s reimbursement but didn’t say whether counties and other taxing entities could continue to offer it if they choose. He added that he does not believe the state should cover those tax credits.
 Department of Corrections
 The Department of Corrections budget for 2027-28 is proposed at $1.4 billion, an increase of about $17 million over 2026-27. Polis said most of those additional funds are to pay for more clinical staff, shift relief and additional caseload. 
 The governor will present his budget proposal to the Joint Budget Committee on Nov. 12.
